paragraphs.source_en: Tokugawa Ieyasu resigned from the office of shogun on the sixteenth day of the fourth month of Keichō 10. Ieyasu had been born on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of Tenbun 11, which made him sixty-two years and a little over one hundred days old. Hideyoshi was reportedly born on the first day of the first month; if that was true, then by the time he died on the eighteenth day of the eighth month of Keichō 3, he had lived sixty-two years and more than two hundred thirty days. Comparing the two, the difference was only a little over one hundred twenty days. What was Ieyasu truly thinking when he relinquished the shogunate before reaching the age at which Hideyoshi had died?

paragraphs.source_en: In human affairs, victory and defeat are ever alternating, as are fortune and misfortune. A great river may surge on without end, while even a tiny stream may overflow and bring disaster. Osaka was the first place where the storm broke, though it was not Osaka alone. Once Tokugawa Hidetada’s host, said to number one hundred sixty thousand, entered Owari, commoners began to flee. To people not yet accustomed to an age of peace, an army of one hundred sixty thousand could only mean that war was about to begin.
